title: Consistency models, CAP, PACELC and conflicts
goal: By the end you can name the consistency model a store gives you and break two of them on a replica set, state CAP and PACELC correctly and place a configuration in PACELC's terms, and say how last write wins, vector clocks and CRDTs each handle two concurrent writes.

warmup.q: Two regions replicate a payments store. The link between them goes down for five minutes; both data centres are healthy. What does CAP say about those five minutes?
options: Nothing: you picked two of the three properties when you chose the database
Each region must either refuse writes it can't confirm with the other, or accept them and let the copies disagree until the link returns
Writes are lost, because eventual consistency drops what it can't replicate
Both regions can stay fully consistent and available if they use quorums
warmup.why: CAP is about exactly this case, a network partition. A replica that can't reach the others either answers, and gives up consistency (linearizability), or refuses, and gives up availability. "Pick two" is a misreading: partitions aren't optional, and CAP says nothing about healthy periods. Eventual consistency is about when copies agree, not about dropping writes, and a quorum can't form across a partition for the side that's in the minority.

sections.h: A consistency model says which writes a read may miss
sections.body:
Lessons 6 and 8 both ended with a read that returned something old: a stale replica at `ONE`, a secondary that hadn't replicated yet. "Stale" isn't precise enough to design with. You need to say which old values a read may return, and that promise is a consistency model. Jepsen defines it as a safety property that "declares what a system can do". The models form a ladder, from the strongest down.

Linearizable: the store behaves as if there were one copy. Every read sees every write that finished before the read started, in real time. If a payment's capture completed at 10:00:00.200, a read that starts at 10:00:00.300 on any replica sees it.

Sequential: everyone sees all writes in one agreed order, but that order may lag real time. Your read can be a little behind, but never shows writes in an order another client wouldn't see.

Causal: writes that depend on each other are seen in order. If you read the authorization and then write the capture, nobody sees the capture without the authorization. Unrelated writes may appear in any order.

Below those sit four session guarantees, promises to one client about its own history. Read your writes: after you write, your reads see it. Monotonic reads: once you've seen a value, you never see an older one. Monotonic writes: your writes apply in the order you sent them. Writes follow reads: a write you make after reading something is ordered after it.

Eventual consistency is the bottom: if writes stop, all replicas end up the same. It says nothing about when, or about what reads show in between. It doesn't mean data loss, a common misreading. Hints, read repair and anti-entropy exist to converge copies, not to drop writes. Writes get lost through specific mechanisms you've already met: a `w: 1` rollback, last write wins discarding a concurrent write (section 3), a tombstone purged before repair.

Strength costs availability, and Jepsen's map says exactly how much. Linearizable and sequential can't be totally available: during a network partition, some replicas must refuse requests. Causal, read your writes and monotonic reads can be at most sticky available: a client that keeps talking to the same replica can keep going. Weaker models can be totally available.

**Every replica holds its own copy of the history of writes. A consistency model says which of those histories a read may show you, and a conflict is two histories that each hold a write the other lacks.** The Try-it breaks two session guarantees on a real replica set.

try.title: Break read-your-writes and monotonic reads
steps: From the `labs` folder, start lesson 8's three-member replica set: `docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml up -d --wait` (about 30 seconds, about 1.5 GB of Docker memory).
Run the commands below. `db.fsyncLock()` makes mongo3 stop applying writes while it keeps answering reads, like a secondary that has fallen behind.
Before the loop, predict what each member says the balance is.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml up -d --wait

# the starting balance, on every member
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.balances.insertOne({_id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: 10000}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority"}})'

# mongo3 stops applying replication (it still answers reads)
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo3 mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncLock().lockCount'

# a 3,000 payment, acknowledged by the primary alone
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.balances.updateOne({_id: "A-1001"}, {$inc: {balanceMinor: -3000}}, {writeConcern: {w: 1}}).modifiedCount'

# a client that reads from whichever member is nearest
for m in mongo1 mongo2 mongo3; do
  docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec $m mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'db.getMongo().setReadPref("nearest"); print(db.hello().me, db.balances.findOne().balanceMinor)'
done

docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo3 mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncUnlock().lockCount'

try.expect:
```text
{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: 'A-1001' }
Long('1')
1
mongo1:27017 7000
mongo2:27017 7000
mongo3:27017 10000
Long('0')
```

mongo3 is frozen against writes, so it never applied the payment. A client that wrote through mongo1 and then read from mongo3 sees its own payment missing: read your writes is broken. A client that reads mongo2 (7000) and then mongo3 (10000) sees the balance go back up: monotonic reads is broken. Nothing failed and no error appeared. MongoDB keeps both promises only for reads from the primary, or in a causally consistent session that reads and writes with `majority`. `fsyncLock` stands in for a slow or partitioned secondary; after the unlock, mongo3 catches up. Leave the set running for the next Try-it.

refs.title: Jepsen: consistency models and their availability

sections.h: CAP is about partitions; PACELC adds the latency you pay every day
sections.body:
CAP is usually quoted as "consistency, availability, partition tolerance: pick any two". That reading is wrong, and Abadi's 2012 paper takes it apart. One concrete case shows what the theorem does say.

Two replicas of A-1001's balance, one in each region, and the link between them goes down. That's a network partition: both machines run fine, but messages between them are lost. A payment arrives at the EU replica. The EU replica can't reach the US one. It has exactly two options. It can answer, applying the payment locally, and then the US replica will serve the old balance until the link returns: available, not consistent. Or it can refuse until it can confirm with the other side: consistent, not available. CAP's consistency means linearizable, and its availability means every live replica answers. During a partition, no design gets both. That's the whole theorem.

So "pick two" misleads twice. Partitions aren't optional; a network that never loses messages doesn't exist, so the real choice is C or A when one happens. And when there's no partition, CAP says nothing at all. Yet replicated stores weaken consistency on healthy days too. Abadi's point is that this comes from a different trade-off: latency. To be consistent a write has to wait for other replicas, and waiting costs time, from a millisecond in one data centre to about 70 ms between regions.

PACELC (say "pass-elk") puts both in one sentence: if there's a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. You've already turned both dials. In lesson 6, `QUORUM` with two Cassandra nodes down refused with `Unavailable` (PC for that request), while `ONE` kept answering (PA). In lesson 8, the cut-off primary stepped down (PC), and `w: "majority"` waited for a second member (EC) where `w: 1` didn't (EL). The Try-it times the EL/EC choice.

Abadi's paper classed systems by their defaults: Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak as PA/EL; BigTable and HBase as PC/EC; Yahoo's PNUTS as PC/EL; and the MongoDB of 2012 as PA/EC. Read those as descriptions of configurations, not of products. MongoDB's default write concern is `majority` today, and Cassandra picks per statement.

try.title: Time the latency and consistency trade
steps: On the same replica set, run the commands below. Predict the time each write takes once both secondaries are frozen, and what `local` and `majority` reads return.
The last command stops the set and deletes its data.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
# healthy set: time both kinds of write (the first one also pays for warming up)
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'for (const w of [1, "majority", 1, "majority"]) { const t = process.hrtime.bigint(); db.balances.updateOne({_id: "A-1001"}, {$inc: {balanceMinor: -1}}, {writeConcern: {w}}); print("w:" + w, Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - t) / 1e6, "ms") }'

# both secondaries stop applying replication: as if the primary were cut off from them
for m in mongo2 mongo3; do docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec $m mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncLock().lockCount'; done

# the same payment, once per write concern, with a 3-second wtimeout
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'for (const w of [1, "majority"]) { const t = process.hrtime.bigint(); try { db.balances.updateOne({_id: "A-1001"}, {$inc: {balanceMinor: -1000}}, {writeConcern: {w, wtimeout: 3000}}); print("w:" + w, "ok") } catch (e) { print("w:" + w, e.message) } print("   ", Math.round(Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - t) / 1e6), "ms") }'

# two read concerns, same primary, same moment
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'for (const level of ["local", "majority"]) print(level, db.balances.find({_id: "A-1001"}).readConcern(level).next().balanceMinor)'

# heal, read again, stop
for m in mongo2 mongo3; do docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec $m mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncUnlock().lockCount'; done
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval 'for (const level of ["local", "majority"]) print(level, db.balances.find({_id: "A-1001"}).readConcern(level).next().balanceMinor)'
docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml down -v

try.expect:
```text
w:1 19.794417 ms
w:majority 6.341291 ms
w:1 1.556042 ms
w:majority 5.253792 ms
Long('1')
Long('1')
w:1 ok
    17 ms
w:majority waiting for replication timed out
    3032 ms
local 4996
majority 6996
Long('0')
Long('0')
local 4996
majority 4996
```

On a healthy set, waiting for a majority cost about 4 ms more than `w: 1`, here between containers on one machine; between regions it would be a round trip of tens of milliseconds. That's the E in PACELC: latency or consistency. With both secondaries frozen, `w: 1` still answered at once (available, and in danger of rollback), while `w: "majority"` waited out its 3 seconds and gave up: the P choice, made per write. The reads show the same split: `local` returned 4996, including two writes no secondary had, while `majority` returned 6996, the last value a majority held. The timed-out write wasn't undone: after the unlock both reads say 4996. Your timings will differ; the gap between the two kinds of write is what to look at.

sections.h: Last write wins drops a write; vector clocks notice it
sections.body:
Two writes are concurrent when neither saw the other: the capture on one replica and the void on another, during a partition or just in the same millisecond. Some rule has to decide what the key holds afterwards. Build the rule up.

Version 1 is last write wins (LWW). Every write carries a timestamp, and the highest timestamp wins on every replica. It's simple, it always converges, and it's Cassandra's rule for every cell (lesson 7). Two things go wrong. Even with perfect clocks it keeps one write and silently drops the other: a capture and a refund issued at the same moment can't both survive. And clocks aren't perfect. NTP keeps servers within milliseconds of each other on a good day, and much worse after a VM pause or a bad time source. With the Java driver stamping writes on the application server, a pod whose clock runs 5 seconds fast wins every argument for 5 seconds. The Try-it does exactly that in Cassandra: the later decision, a void, loses to an earlier capture.

Version 2 notices the problem instead of hiding it. A vector clock is a list of (node, counter) pairs, one for each node that has coordinated a write of this value. When node Sx coordinates a write, it takes the clock of the version the client read and adds 1 to its own entry. To compare two versions, compare entry by entry, treating a missing node as 0. If every entry of A is at most B's, A is an ancestor: B saw it, so A can go. If each has an entry bigger than the other's, the versions are concurrent.

The Dynamo paper walks through this with a shopping cart. D1 and D2 are written through Sx, so D2 is `[(Sx, 2)]`. Two clients both read D2 and write at the same time, one through Sy and one through Sz: D3 is `[(Sx, 2), (Sy, 1)]`, D4 is `[(Sx, 2), (Sz, 1)]`, and neither is an ancestor of the other. Dynamo keeps both as siblings and returns both on the next read. The client merges the carts and writes D5 through Sx with the merged clock as context: `[(Sx, 3), (Sy, 1), (Sz, 1)]`, which descends from both and replaces them.

Vector clocks detect conflicts; they don't resolve them. Your code gets siblings and has to merge them, and the obvious merge has a flaw the stepper shows: a set union brings deleted items back. Clocks also grow with every node that coordinates a write, which is why Dynamo truncated them at about 10 entries. Section 4 removes the merge code.

frames.say: The link comes back. With last write wins, the replicas compare wall-clock timestamps and keep the later value whole. EU wrote at 10:00:05 by its clock, US at 10:00:03 by its own, so US's version disappears, and with it the block on card-5310. No error, no log line. If EU's clock was a few seconds fast, the "later" write wasn't even later.

frames.say: Vector clocks don't trust wall clocks. Compare the two entry by entry: EU's counter for `eu` is bigger, US's counter for `us` is bigger. Neither clock is less than or equal to the other in every entry, so neither write saw the other. They're concurrent, and Dynamo keeps both as siblings for the application to merge, as in its D1 to D5 example.

frames.say: The application has to merge the siblings. The obvious merge, a set union, keeps card-5310, but it also brings card-4417 back, because a missing element can mean "removed" or "never added" and the union can't tell which. That's the Dynamo paper's own warning about the shopping cart: an added item is never lost, but a deleted item can resurface.

sections.h: CRDTs merge in any order without losing a write
sections.body:
Merging siblings by hand is where conflict handling usually breaks. What if the data type knew how to merge itself, so that any two copies combine into the same result in any order, and no write is lost? That's a CRDT, a conflict-free replicated data type, and the idea is easiest to see with a counter.

Count M-0042's pending payouts in three regions during a partition. Version 1 gives each replica one running total, and merging two copies adds their totals. That double-counts: once EU has merged US's total, the next sync between them adds US's payouts a second time, and copies that reach EU by two paths count twice too. Version 2 is the G-Counter (grow-only counter): every replica owns one slot and only increments its own. The value is the sum of the slots, and two copies merge by taking the maximum of each slot. A slot only grows, so the bigger number is always the newer one, and taking it twice changes nothing. To count down as well, keep two G-Counters, one for increments and one for decrements, and subtract: a PN-Counter.

The maximum works because it has three properties: the order of merges doesn't matter (commutative), the grouping doesn't matter (associative), and repeating a merge changes nothing (idempotent). Any merge with those three properties lets replicas exchange state whenever they can, through any path, as often as they like, and still converge. No clock is involved, and nobody waits for anyone.

Sets are harder, because removals are where unions fail. The OR-Set (observed-remove set) tags every add with a unique tag, such as `us:1`. A remove records the tags of that element it has seen, and only those. An element is in the set if it has a tag nobody removed. Merging is two unions, of tags and of removed tags. A remove beats the adds it saw, and a concurrent add, which it couldn't see, survives. In the Try-it, one region unblocks card-4417 while another blocks it again, and after the merge it's blocked.

CRDTs have limits that matter in payments. Their metadata grows: slots per replica, a tag per add, removed tags kept forever unless the replicas coordinate to clean them up. And they only fit operations that commute. "Balance never goes below zero" doesn't: two regions can each approve a 600 payment from a balance of 1,000, and both counters merge happily to -200. An invariant like that needs replicas that agree before they write, which is the subject of lesson 10. CRDTs suit counts, sets, flags and collaborative documents. Riak added them as built-in data types in version 2.0, and libraries such as Automerge use them for collaborative editing.

try.title: Three regions diverge, then merge in every order

Predict the merged count and the merged set before you run it. Then run it from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed.

code.title: CrdtDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
eu sees pending payouts = 6
us sees pending payouts = 9
ap sees pending payouts = 4
eu sees blocked cards = [card-9921]
us sees blocked cards = [card-4417, card-5310, card-9921]
ap sees blocked cards = [card-4417]
after the partition heals:
  merge eu + us + ap -> pending payouts = 9
  merge eu + ap + us -> pending payouts = 9
  merge us + eu + ap -> pending payouts = 9
  merge us + ap + eu -> pending payouts = 9
  merge ap + eu + us -> pending payouts = 9
  merge ap + us + eu -> pending payouts = 9
  merge eu + us + ap -> blocked cards = [card-4417, card-5310]
  (the other five orders print the same set)
```

5 + 3 - 2 + 4 - 1 = 9: every increment and decrement counted once, in every order. card-9921 is gone, because ap's remove had seen its only tag. card-4417 is back in the set: eu removed tag `eu:1`, but us had blocked it again with a new tag, `us:1`, that eu never saw, so the concurrent add wins. Change one region's edits in the demo and check that all six orders still agree.

refs.title: crdt.tech: papers, implementations and a glossary of CRDTs

analogy: Think of two branch offices that keep the same list of blocked cards, and phone each other with changes. When the phone line is down, each office can keep working from its own list, and they'll disagree for a while (availability), or stop changing the list until the line is back (consistency): that's CAP. Even with the line up, phoning before every change makes each change slower, and not phoning makes the lists differ for a moment: that's PACELC's other half. When they reconcile, comparing the time on each office's wall clock is last write wins, and a fast clock wins every argument. Each office keeping a count of the changes it made is a vector clock, which spots that both changed the list while apart. Keeping a ticket for every entry and every crossing-out lets them merge without arguing, which is a CRDT. The analogy breaks on scale: real replicas reconcile thousands of times a second, with no one to phone, so the merge rule has to be decided before the conflict happens.
in_your_world: Your payments service makes these choices whether you name them or not. Reading a balance from a MongoDB secondary or at Cassandra `ONE` gives up read-your-writes, so a customer can pay and then see the old balance; route decision-making reads to the primary or to `QUORUM`. Every Cassandra update your Quarkus pods send is stamped with the pod's clock, so a pod with a drifting clock silently wins or loses writes; alert on NTP offset like you alert on heap. When you consider an active-active setup across two regions, ask which data can be a CRDT (counters for dashboards, sets of blocked cards, feature flags) and which needs one place to decide (balances, idempotency keys, payment status). The second kind belongs in a single-leader store or behind a transaction, the subject of lesson 10. A Kafka topic per payment, consumed in order, is one more way to get a single order of writes per key.
mistake: The most common mistake is reading CAP as "pick any two" and concluding that a CP database is always consistent and an AP one always loses data. People do it because the triangle diagram is everywhere. In fact CAP only describes what happens during a partition, and most of the trade-offs you live with are PACELC's latency ones on normal days: Cassandra at `ONE`, MongoDB with `w: 1` or secondary reads. And "eventual" doesn't mean lossy; loss comes from specific mechanisms such as last write wins with skewed clocks or a rolled-back `w: 1` write. The fix: for each piece of data, name the consistency model you need (linearizable for a balance check, read-your-writes for a payment screen, eventual for a dashboard), then check which setting of your store gives it and what it costs.

compare.title: Two concurrent updates: last write wins and vector clocks

a.label: Last write wins (Cassandra)
a.src:
capture   status = CAPTURED   ts 10:00:05 (server 2, clock +5 s)
void      status = VOIDED     ts 10:00:02 (server 1, clock right)

every replica keeps the higher timestamp:
  status = CAPTURED
  the void is gone; no error, no sibling, no trace

b.label: Vector clocks (Dynamo)
b.src:
both servers read version [(s1, 1)]
capture   [(s1, 1), (s2, 1)]
void      [(s1, 2)]

compare: s1 is bigger in one, s2 in the other -> CONCURRENT
the next read returns BOTH as siblings:
  CAPTURED [(s1, 1), (s2, 1)]  and  VOIDED [(s1, 2)]
the application decides, and writes back with [(s1, 2), (s2, 1)]

compare.note: Last write wins always produces one answer, so applications never see a conflict, and that's exactly the problem: it decides by clock readings, and one of two concurrent writes disappears. Vector clocks never pick by time. They tell you that two writes didn't see each other, and hand both to your code, which then needs a merge rule that is right for the data. For payment status neither is good enough: the void and the capture shouldn't both be accepted, which needs a check before writing (a lightweight transaction or a single leader), not a merge after.

lab.title: Build vector clocks, a last-write-wins register and three CRDTs
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. No Docker needed. All ten fail.
In `VectorClock.kt`, write `compare` and `merge`, then `DynamoKey.put`. `prune`, `receive` and `context` are given. Four tests pass, including Dynamo's D1 to D5 example, replica by replica.
In `Crdts.kt`, write `LwwRegister.merge`. Its test passes and shows the skewed-clock loss from the Try-it; the next test shows vector clocks calling the same two writes concurrent.

Write `GCounter.merge`, then the OR-Set's `remove`, `elements` and `merge`. The last test makes 40 random edits on three replicas, syncs some of them in random directions, and checks that all six merge orders agree, fifty times.
Experiment: change `GCounter.merge` to add the slots instead of taking the maximum, and see which tests fail and why. Put it back.
hints: In `compare`, loop over `counters.keys + other.counters.keys` and set two flags: `smaller` if `this[node] < other[node]`, `bigger` if `>`. Both: CONCURRENT. Only smaller: BEFORE. Only bigger: AFTER. Neither: EQUAL.
`merge` is `(counters.keys + other.counters.keys).associateWith { maxOf(this[it], other[it]) }`, wrapped in a `VectorClock`.
`put` is three lines: `Version(value, context.increment(node))`, then `versions = prune(versions + written)`, then return it.
LWW: compare `timestamp` first; on a tie compare `node`, so every replica picks the same winner whatever order it merges in.
OR-Set `remove` adds `adds[element].orEmpty()` to `removed`. `elements` keeps the keys of `adds` whose tags aren't all in `removed`. `merge` unions the tag sets per element and unions `removed`.
lab.done_when: All ten tests in `VectorClockTest` and `CrdtTest` pass.

drill.title: Compare clocks and merge counters by hand
drill.prompt: Without running anything, answer: (a) how `[(Sx, 2), (Sy, 1)]` relates to `[(Sx, 2), (Sz, 1)]`, to `[(Sx, 3), (Sy, 1)]` and to `[(Sx, 1)]`; (b) the clock of a write coordinated by Sz whose client read both of the first two; (c) the merge of the G-Counters `{eu: 4, us: 2}` and `{eu: 3, us: 5, ap: 1}`, and its value; (d) PACELC in one sentence.

answer.src:
(a) [(Sx,2),(Sy,1)] vs [(Sx,2),(Sz,1)]   CONCURRENT  (bigger on Sy, smaller on Sz)
    [(Sx,2),(Sy,1)] vs [(Sx,3),(Sy,1)]   BEFORE      (every entry <=, one smaller)
    [(Sx,2),(Sy,1)] vs [(Sx,1)]          AFTER       (every entry >=, Sx bigger)
(b) context = merge = [(Sx,2),(Sy,1),(Sz,1)]; Sz increments its own entry:
    [(Sx,2),(Sy,1),(Sz,2)]
(c) max per slot: {eu: 4, us: 5, ap: 1}, value 10   (adding the slots would give 15: wrong)
(d) If there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency;
    Else, choose Latency or Consistency.

recap: A consistency model says which writes a read may miss. From strongest: linearizable (like one copy, real time), sequential, causal, then session guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads and writes, writes follow reads), then eventual.

Stronger models cost availability: linearizable and sequential can't stay totally available in a partition; causal and the session guarantees can at most be sticky available. Eventual consistency is about when copies agree, not about losing data.
CAP: during a partition, a replica either answers (available) or refuses (consistent); it says nothing about normal days. PACELC adds the everyday trade: else, latency or consistency.

Last write wins converges but drops one of two concurrent writes, and with client timestamps a fast clock wins. Vector clocks detect concurrency by comparing (node, counter) entries and return siblings for the application to merge.

CRDTs merge by operations that are commutative, associative and idempotent: G-Counter (max per slot), PN-Counter (two G-Counters), OR-Set (unique tags, remove what you saw). They don't fit invariants like "balance never below zero".

quiz.q: A Cassandra keyspace has three replicas, and two are cut off from the coordinator. A read at `QUORUM` fails with `Unavailable`; the same read at `ONE` returns a balance. In CAP's terms, what happened?
options: Cassandra is AP, so the QUORUM failure is a bug
Cassandra is CP, so the ONE read must be linearizable
Each request chose: QUORUM refused rather than risk a stale answer (C), ONE answered from what it had (A)
CAP doesn't apply, because only two nodes are down
quiz.why: CAP describes a choice made during a partition, and Cassandra lets each statement make it. QUORUM can't reach a majority, so it refuses: consistency over availability. ONE answers from one replica that may be stale: availability over consistency. Labels such as "Cassandra is AP" describe defaults, not every request.

quiz.q: With no failures at all, a team switches from `w: 1` to `w: "majority"` and writes get about 4 ms slower. Which part of PACELC is that?
options: EC: else, choosing consistency over latency
PC: choosing consistency during a partition
PA: choosing availability during a partition
None: PACELC only covers failures
quiz.why: There's no partition, so it's the E half: with everything healthy, waiting for a second member trades latency for the guarantee that the write survives a failover. The Try-it measured about 1.6 ms against 5.3 ms between containers; across regions the gap is a round trip. CAP alone has nothing to say about this.

quiz.q: A customer pays 3,000 through the primary, then the app reads the balance from a secondary that's behind and shows the old 10,000. Then a refresh hits another secondary and shows 7,000, and a third refresh hits the first one again and shows 10,000. Which guarantees were broken?
options: Only linearizability; session guarantees hold for every MongoDB read
Read your writes (the customer's own payment was missing) and monotonic reads (the balance went from 7,000 back to 10,000)
Only eventual consistency, because the copies disagreed
None: secondaries are allowed to be behind, so nothing was promised
quiz.why: The customer wrote, then didn't see the write: read your writes. They saw 7,000, then an older 10,000: monotonic reads. Eventual consistency still holds, since the copies converge once replication catches up. Reading from the primary, or using a causally consistent session with majority reads and writes, keeps both promises.

quiz.q: Two copies of a G-Counter are `{eu: 5, us: 2}` and `{eu: 3, us: 4}`. Why does the merge take `{eu: 5, us: 4}` rather than adding to `{eu: 8, us: 6}`?
options: Because adding would overflow the counter
Because the maximum is faster to compute
Because each slot only grows, so the bigger value already includes the smaller, and adding would count the same increments twice
Because CRDTs never store more than one value per slot
quiz.why: eu's slot is only ever incremented by eu, so 5 is a later state of the same slot than 3, and contains those 3 increments. Taking the maximum gives the same result in any order and when repeated, which lets copies sync any number of times. Adding counts shared history twice: merge the same copy again and the total keeps climbing.

quiz.q: From lesson 6: Cassandra with N = 3, every write and read at `QUORUM`. Is that linearizable?
options: Yes: R + W > N means every read sees every write
No: R + W > N makes acknowledged writes and reads overlap, but timeouts, concurrent writes resolved by timestamp and reads during a write still break the one-copy illusion
Yes, as long as hinted handoff is on
No, because QUORUM reads only ask one replica
quiz.why: Lesson 6 showed the overlap guarantee and its gaps: a timed-out write may still land, two concurrent writes are settled by timestamps (last write wins), and a quorum read during a write can see it while a later one doesn't, unless read repair blocks. Abadi: "simply using a quorum protocol is not sufficient" for linearizability. Cassandra's lightweight transactions add the missing agreement step.

flashcards.back: The store behaves like one copy: every read sees every write that completed before the read began, in real time.

flashcards.front: Read your writes vs monotonic reads?
flashcards.back: Read your writes: after you write, your reads include it. Monotonic reads: once you've seen a value, you never see an older one.
During a network partition, a replica that can't reach the others must either answer (give up linearizability) or refuse (give up availability). Nothing about normal operation.
If Partition: Availability or Consistency. Else: Latency or Consistency. Abadi, 2012.

flashcards.front: How do you compare two vector clocks?
flashcards.back: Entry by entry, missing = 0. All <= with one smaller: ancestor. Each bigger somewhere: concurrent, keep both as siblings.

flashcards.front: Why does last write wins lose data?
flashcards.back: It keeps one of two concurrent writes by timestamp and drops the other silently, and a skewed clock can make the earlier write win.

flashcards.front: What makes a CRDT merge safe?
flashcards.back: It's commutative, associative and idempotent, so copies converge whatever order and however often they merge. Example: G-Counter takes the max per slot.

terms.plain: A promise about which writes a read may or may not reflect; Jepsen: a safety property that declares what a system can do.
The strongest single-object model: the store behaves like one copy, and reads see every write that finished before they started.
Promises to one client about its own history: read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes follow reads.
Machines keep running but messages between groups of them are lost.
Abadi's extension of CAP: in a partition, availability or consistency; else, latency or consistency.
Conflict rule that keeps the value with the highest timestamp and drops the rest.
A list of (node, counter) pairs on each version; comparing two shows whether one saw the other or they're concurrent.
Conflict-free replicated data type: a value whose merge gives the same result in any order, so replicas converge without coordination.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says: "CAP means we pick two. We picked availability and partition tolerance with Cassandra, so we accept that data gets lost sometimes." Explain what CAP and PACELC really say, and where data loss in such a setup actually comes from.
explain_back.answer: CAP only talks about a network partition. When replicas can't reach each other, each one either keeps answering, and the copies can disagree, or refuses until it can confirm, and that's the whole choice. Partitions aren't something you opt out of, and CAP says nothing about normal days. PACELC adds the everyday half: even with a healthy network, waiting for other replicas costs latency, so you trade latency for consistency. Cassandra lets each statement choose: QUORUM refuses during a partition that leaves it without a majority, and ONE keeps answering. Choosing availability doesn't mean losing data; eventual consistency means copies converge later, and hints, read repair and repair make sure they do. Data gets lost through specific mechanisms. Last write wins keeps one of two concurrent writes and drops the other, and with client-side timestamps a pod whose clock runs fast wins every argument. A tombstone purged before repair brings a deleted row back. So we should name what each table needs, use QUORUM and lightweight transactions where two writers can race, keep NTP healthy, and use CRDT-style data, like counters with one slot per writer, where both writes should survive.

deeper.body:
Gilbert and Lynch proved CAP in 2002, for a precise model: consistency means linearizability, and availability means every request to a non-failing node gets a response. Much of the confusion around CAP comes from people using everyday meanings for those words. A system can be neither CAP-consistent nor CAP-available, and most real configurations are: Cassandra at QUORUM refuses in a minority partition and still isn't linearizable.

Abadi's PACELC paper has a case worth studying: Yahoo's PNUTS, which he classed PC/EL, and called that label "admittedly somewhat confusing". PNUTS keeps a master copy per record; normally reads may be served by any replica and be stale (EL), but during a partition it reduces availability rather than let records diverge (PC). If you can explain why PC doesn't mean "fully consistent" there, you understand the framework rather than the acronym.

Vector clocks have a cousin you'll meet in lesson 10's reading and in Kafka: version vectors track versions of one replicated value, while vector clocks in the original sense track causality between events in processes. Dynamo's clocks are what most people now call version vectors. Riak replaced plain vector clocks with dotted version vectors to avoid sibling explosion when many clients write through one node.

CRDTs come in two styles. State-based CRDTs, the ones in this lesson's lab, ship the whole state and merge it. Operation-based CRDTs ship each operation and need a delivery layer that delivers every operation exactly once, in causal order. Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero and Zawirski's 2011 report, "A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types", defines both and catalogues counters, registers, sets, graphs and sequences; crdt.tech links it and much more. The hard parts in practice are garbage-collecting tags and removed markers, and designing data so that the invariants you care about are ones a merge can keep.
